title: When something goes wrong
job: Problems, asking for help, complaining calmly
verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: Mir ist schlecht / Ich habe Kopfschmerzen

rules.text: helfen TAKES THE DATIVE, and it is not alone: helfen, danken, gefallen, gehören and passen all take a dative object where English takes a plain one. Ich helfe Ihnen, never Ich helfe Sie. No rule predicts membership, so it is learnt as a list — a short one — and this is M3's article grid earning its keep a second time.

Mir ist schlecht has NO GRAMMATICAL SUBJECT AT ALL. L1-M9 already shipped one of these — Mir ist kalt — without naming the pattern; naming it here makes the whole family fall out at once: Mir ist warm, Mir ist schlecht, Mir tut der Kopf weh. German, Russian and Italian all put the person in an oblique case for how they feel, and a learner shown the connection back to L1-M9 learns one thing instead of four.

kein AGAINST nicht, and L1 shipped both halves without ever stating the rule. kein negates a noun that would take ein or no article at all: Ich habe kein Geld, Das ist kein Problem. nicht negates everything else — a verb, an adjective, or a noun that already has a definite article: Es funktioniert nicht, Der Bus kommt nicht. It is one of the few German rules with a clean statement, and an English speaker who has only "not" will reach for nicht everywhere.

Complaining calmly is a register lesson, and German's answer is closer to Russian's than to English's: the softening is the OPENING — Entschuldigung, … — and the word leider, not a weakening of the claim itself. Es funktioniert nicht is a normal thing to say and is not rude. An English speaker's "there seems to be a slight issue" reads as evasive rather than polite, and neither language is being judged here.

Body parts take a DEFINITE article where English takes a possessive: Mir tut der Kopf weh, not mein Kopf. The dative already says whose it is, so the possessive would be saying it twice. Ich habe Kopfschmerzen is the other way to say the same thing and is if anything commoner.

words.note: Only of machines and arrangements. A person who works is arbeiten, and using funktionieren of somebody is as strange in German as it would be in English.

words.note: The possessive takes the SAME endings as ein, so M3's grid decides it: der Schlüssel is the object here, so mein grows the accusative -en.
Masculine, and its plural is also Schlüssel. The ü is said with the lips of an oo and the tongue of an ee.
Its participle verloren goes to the very end, which is M1's bracket doing the past. ver- is never stressed, so nothing splits off it.
Spelled the same as an infinitive and as a participle, because ver- verbs take no ge-. Losing a key and forgetting one are different sentences with the same shape.

sentences.trap: The participle waits at the END, exactly as an infinitive does behind a modal. Ich habe verloren meinen Schlüssel is the English order and is not German.

words.note: Mir ist schlecht is nausea and nothing else. Es ist schlecht, with a subject, is a judgement about a thing — one adjective, two sentences that share no meaning at all.

sentences.trap: There is no subject here and there cannot be one. Ich bin schlecht means you are a bad person, and it is one of the most costly single-word slips an English speaker can make in German.

words.note: The one softener German reaches for, and it sits inside the sentence rather than in front of it. Leider nicht on its own is a complete and gentle no.
L1-M1's kommen in its third person. Of a bus or a train it means arriving at all, not arriving here — Der Bus kommt nicht is the announcement you will hear.

sentences.trap: Der Bus is definite, so it takes NICHT — and kommen of a bus means arriving at all rather than arriving here. Swap in a bare noun and the negation changes with it: Es gibt keinen Bus.

words.note: Blunt, everyday and not at all rude — it is what a landlord expects to hear. Its stress is on the second syllable, which is unusual for so short a word.
Feminine, from heiß. Nouns in -ung are feminine without exception, which is the one gender rule in German worth memorising.

words.note: It takes M3's accusative — einen Arzt — and it is a plain verb, not a modal, so a following verb would need zu. At this level it takes nouns only.
Masculine, and the feminine is Ärztin with the umlaut. Both are one index key apart, because the fold keeps umlauts.
